newsitem.title: TAIWAN: C.Americans open Taiwan trade office to boost ties.
newsitem.headline: C.Americans open Taiwan trade office to boost ties.

text.p: Five Central American states on Tuesday opened a Taipei trade office and Taiwan reciprocated by kicking in half of a US$200 million development fund as the allies closed ranks after Hong Kong's absorption by China.

Envoys from the five said diplomatic ties with Taiwan would remain unchanged in the face of growing pressure from Beijing, which is forcing them to downgrade or even close their Hong Kong consulates because of their formal links with Taipei.
"The return of Hong Kong (to Beijing) should not have any impact on bilateral relations (with Taiwan)," Nicaragua's Taipei ambassador Salvador Stadthagen told a reception.
"Our business will be as usual," he said.
Beijing has regarded Taiwan as a renegade province since a 1949 civil war split and sees Hong Kong's return as a model for the island's eventual "reunification with the motherland".
Costa Rican ambassador Elena Wachong said the new Taipei trade office would bolster investment and tourism ties in the wake of Hong Kong's sovereignty shift a few hours earlier.
"This opens a new door for our relationship," Wachong said on behalf of the five. "We are offering opportunities for Taiwan to diversify investment and strengthen diplomatic ties."
Also involved are El Salvador, Guatemala and Honduras.
The five are among just 30 states that recognise Taiwan's exiled Republic of China rather than the rival People's Republic in Beijing, which refuses ties with such states.

Top economic policymaker Chiang Pin-kung of the cabinet's Council for Economic Planning and Development announced plans for a free trade pact with Central America -- and contribution of US$100 million over 10 years to a US$200 million fund to help the region's development.
Chiang said Taiwan would use Central America as a bridge to promote trade in North and South America.
Economics minister Wang Chih-kang said exports to the five nations accounted for only 0.3 percent of total Taiwan trade, while imports from the five represented only 0.02 percent.
"We still have large room to develop," Wang said.
Taiwan's 1996 exports hit US$116.1 billion, while imports were US$102.1 billion.

Central bank governor Sheu Yuan-dong said helping the five countries set up the trade office aimed to offer more practical help instead of simply offering loans or aids to them. "We want to help them catch fish, not give them fish," Sheu said.
Taiwan is a member of the Central American Bank of Economic Integration, the only international organisation that allows Taiwan to use its official name -- Republic of China.
Deputy Foreign Minister Chen Chien-jen stressed the importance of keeping ties with the Central America, calling them Taiwan's "most important" allies.
